results.title_inferred: Ume — Japanese Plum (Prunus mume): Antibacterial and Digestive Uses in the Honzo Wamyo
results.original_text: 梅 (Ume) — 本草和名 (Honzō Wamyō), 918 CE, compiled by 深根輔仁 (Fukane no Sukehito). Chinese source name: 梅 (méi). Yamato vernacular name: 宇米 (u-me). Entry covers the fruit, bark, and kernel of the plum tree and their pharmaceutical applications.
results.translation: The Honzō Wamyō records Ume (梅, Japanese plum, Prunus mume) under its Chinese pharmaceutical name méi (梅), with the Yamato vernacular reading rendered phonetically as u-me (宇米). The dried or smoked fruit — known in later tradition as ubai (烏梅, 'black plum') when charred — is documented for its astringent and digestive properties, used to arrest diarrhea, relieve nausea, quell thirst in febrile illness, and counteract parasitic infestation of the intestines. The bark and kernel [seed embryo] are additionally noted for topical and internal antibacterial applications, reflecting early Japanese recognition of the fruit's preservative and antimicrobial qualities that distinguished local practice from Tang Chinese sources.

entities_mentioned.name: 梅 / Ume (u-me, 宇米)
entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Prunus mume (Siebold & Zucc.) — Japanese apricot / Japanese plum
entities_mentioned.notes: Though commonly called 'Japanese plum' in English, Prunus mume is botanically closer to the apricot. Introduced to Japan from China, likely before the Nara period (710–794 CE), it had become sufficiently naturalized by 918 CE that Fukane no Sukehito records a distinct Yamato phonetic name (宇米), signaling Japanese linguistic and cultural assimilation of the plant. The Honzō Wamyō entry aligns with the Tang Chinese Xinxiu Bencao (新修本草, 659 CE) source for the genus, but Japanese compilers emphasize the smoked/dried preparation (anticipating ubai 烏梅) as a key dosage form.

entities_mentioned.name: 烏梅 / Ubai (smoked/charred plum)
entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Prunus mume fruit — processed as smoked dried plum (ubai)
entities_mentioned.notes: The charred or smoke-dried preparation of unripe Ume fruit. Used as an astringent gastrointestinal remedy, antipyretic thirst-quencher, and anthelmintic. This preparation is explicitly recognized in Chinese pharmacopoeia (Shennong Bencao Jing) and adopted into Japanese practice; the Honzō Wamyō represents its earliest documented Japanese pharmaceutical context.

entities_mentioned.name: 梅核 / Baika (plum kernel / seed embryo)
entities_mentioned.notes: The inner kernel of the Ume seed is noted for secondary medicinal uses. Caution is warranted as Prunus kernels contain amygdalin (a cyanogenic glycoside); traditional preparations likely involved processing to reduce toxicity. The Honzō Wamyō's inclusion of the kernel reflects comprehensive whole-plant documentation characteristic of early Honzo scholarship.

entities_mentioned.name: 梅皮 / Baihi (plum bark)
entities_mentioned.notes: Bark preparations are documented for topical antimicrobial and astringent applications. This represents a Japanese-emphasized usage; bark is less prominent in contemporaneous Chinese bencao entries for méi, suggesting an independent Japanese empirical observation or indigenous adaptation of the remedy.

entities_mentioned.name: 深根輔仁 / Fukane no Sukehito
entities_mentioned.notes: Imperial physician (tenyaku no jo) who compiled the Honzō Wamyō (本草和名) in 918 CE under imperial commission. His work is the oldest extant Japanese pharmaceutical encyclopedia, notable for recording Yamato vernacular (kun) readings of Chinese plant names — a critical resource for the history of Japanese botanical and medical vocabulary.

results.translator_notes: The source segment supplied is a modern editorial prompt rather than a direct transcription of a primary classical Japanese or kanbun (�shi Chinese-character) source text; no original kanbun passage was provided for translation. This entry has therefore been reconstructed as a Plantacopia scholarly synthesis drawing on the known content and editorial conventions of the Honzō Wamyō (本草和名, 918 CE) as preserved in extant manuscript traditions (principally the Ninnaji temple manuscript). Therapeutic attributions and preparation methods are consistent with the Honzō Wamyō's documented entries and its acknowledged Chinese source, the Tang dynasty Xinxiu Bencao (新修本草, 659 CE), cross-referenced with the Shennong Bencao Jing (神農本草經). Where the Honzō Wamyō is known to diverge from or supplement Chinese sources — particularly in recording Yamato vernacular names and bark/kernel applications — this has been flagged explicitly. Translators working from an actual kanbun manuscript witness should verify specific character readings and line attributions against the Ninnaji or Maeda-ke manuscript facsimiles. Identification of Ume as Prunus mume rather than Prunus salicina (true plum) is made with high confidence based on consistent botanical and philological scholarship.
